_readme: Copy to config.json, or just run PhantomMonitor and pick your display from the tray menu - it writes this file for you. Run 'python phantommonitor.py --list' to see the hardware id of each display.
_blocked_help: 'ABC1234' always blocks that display. 'ABC1234@interlaced' blocks it only while its EDID asks for an interlaced mode - the right rule for a receiver that advertises 1080p with a screen awake behind it and 1080i once that screen is off. 'ABC1234@<1280x720' blocks it only while smaller than that (compared by area), useful when the phantom sits at a small resolution and a real screen behind it would be larger, so the guard stands aside by itself. 'ABC1234@800x600' blocks it only at exactly that size. Run 'python phantommonitor.py --diag' and it will suggest the rule for your hardware. Check what your amp reports first: some advertise 1920x1080 with nothing attached, and then only an id rule or a manual tick will do.
_parked_help: Rules removed by unticking a display are kept here verbatim, so re-ticking restores the exact rule rather than a bare hardware id.
_app_displays_help: Send named apps to a display and keep them there, e.g. {"discord.exe": "GSM7814"}. They open on that display, reopen where you last left them, and are never evacuated from it even when it is blocked - so one screen can be dedicated to them while everything else is kept off. Placement happens when a window opens; drag it elsewhere afterwards and it stays put.
_hotkeys_help: Any mix of ctrl/alt/shift/win plus a letter, digit, F-key or named key (left right up down home end pageup pagedown space insert delete esc tab pause break). Empty string disables one. Matched combos are SWALLOWED and never reach the focused app, so avoid combos your games or apps use.
_hotkey_targets_help: Optional. Pins a hotkey to a display's hardware id, e.g. {"2": "ABC1234"}. Display numbers get reassigned when you plug things in, so a number alone can start meaning a different physical screen; a hardware id never changes.
_av_help: Hardware ids you have declared yourself to be an amp, switch or extractor rather than a display, and ids wrongly guessed as one that you want left alone. These only change the label shown next to a display - NOTHING is ever blocked on this basis. not_av_devices wins over av_devices and over the built-in vendor list.
_cursor_lock_help: Holding the pointer INSIDE an app, which is the opposite of fencing it out of a blocked display. cursor_lock_fullscreen holds it inside a genuinely full-screen borderless app, so mouse-look in a game cannot slide onto another screen. cursor_lock_apps names apps that should hold it whatever their shape. cursor_never_lock names apps that must never hold it - Remote Desktop is first, because holding the pointer inside a full-screen session would strand it away from every other screen.
_updates_help: Off by default: a tray utility should not contact a server unasked. When on, it asks GitHub once at startup whether there is a newer release. 'Check for updates' in the tray menu does the same thing on demand.
_zoom_help: Zoom for the settings window only, 1.0 to 3.0. The control inside that window sets it; Windows' own DPI scaling is honoured on top.
_editor_help: Editor for the tray's 'Edit settings' and 'View log' items. Empty means notepad.exe, which every Windows install has. A name on PATH or a full path both work.
_support_help: A donate or sponsor link for the tray menu. Leave empty and the menu item does not appear at all.
